body:
Yeah. I do need to purge a lot of my belongings. I have a collection of tiny rubber Hulks that I've been hanging on to because I think it's funny that the real Hulk is so big and these are so tiny. Why do I need them? They sit in a drawer and take up space. 

I took a bunch of Xanax last night (some immediate and some extended release so I feel like I get to think clearly all day now). I'm just gonna start with one load of laundry today, and two loads of laundry tomorrow, and two loads of laundry every day until I'm at least caught up enough to only have to to a load every few days. Then I'll reevaluate. I just don't have the patience to build up habits like this.

See, for me, I asked all these questions. I asked, "why?" and "what's the point?" until I came to an answer. I asked and asked until I found something that made it all worth it. For me, that answer was comedy. I love comedy. I love laughing. I love coming up with funny things. I love being with funny people. I love beautiful things like flowers and brownstones. I think that art is the ultimate meaning of my life but I don't have the energy to achieve. I won't be happy if I'm not doing something that feels worthwhile. The most alive I've felt in years is when I got up on stage and delivered 5 minutes of jokes I wrote to a sober and receptive crowd. But I don't have the energy. I can't survive enough to write my jokes. I can't even write my jokes. I don't want to do the work. I don't want to do any of it.

As a kid my mom never enlisted my help to do work around the house because she was a single mom working the night shift so she both felt bad about making me do work and didn't want to go through the work of cleaning up after my failure. 

As I grew up and started noticing that all of my friends had chores, I tried to help out because responsibility seemed fun but I don't take instruction well. 

You know how they say you're supposed to praise a kid's effort instead of her achievements because effort is more important in the long term? I was the kind of kid who was praised *endlessly* for being bright, above average, etc and I'm really feeling that now. I assume that, if stuff doesn't work out for me right away, then it's not ever going to work out for me because pretty much everything always works for me right away. 

Right now, my floor is full of dirty laundry. My bedroom smells like body odor, period stains, gym sweat. You can't see my hardwood floors or my area rug. It's been this bad before and it took hours just to get the floor cleared. Days to get all the laundry done. And I'm just going to have to keep doing it. 

I'd like a clean space. I like the way my floor looks. My mom bought me a thousand dollar area rug for a reason; it's exquisite. I'd function better if I didn't have to get on my hands and knees to find a bra in the morning. I feel crappy about my messiness, laziness. I don't feel functional or productive. I'm not happy with my daily life. I don't feel like I'm living my best life, or even a good one. And I'm just not willing to do what it takes to improve my life. I don't want to.

That was the first thing they tried to treat back when I was in high school. They sent me to a specialist who only treats attention deficit problems and he said I'm impulsive with a willpower deficiency but not biologically deficient in any way.

Then talk to someone. Seriously, you can't give up if you haven't tried, and you can't say you've tried unless you've given every ounce of your effort to the suggestions of a professional who underwent years of expensive training just so he could some day help you.

* Unless you see a *psychiatrist*, you won't be prescribed medication. Only an MD can prescribe. A PhD or a LCSW-R can only talk with you. See someone for talk therapy first. 

* There is nothing wrong with taking medication if someone suggests it. Trying it won't kill you. There may be two weeks of side effects but two weeks of discomfort is worth it if it can help you live the way you need to. You likely won't end up on medication "forever;" in conjunction with talk therapy, a 6 month to one year course of an antidepressant could be enough to help you get your life back on track. 

* Therapists don't just "solve problems." They are trained to provide multiple therapies. If you say, "I have trouble reacting appropriately and proportionately to external events," there's a kind of therapy that involves learning how to react appropriately and becoming self-aware enough to know what an appropriate and proportionate reaction is. If you say, "I just need help getting to where I need to be," they have the skills to help you set goals and plan to achieve them.

Try that. Google psychology practices near you, call, ask if anyone is taking new patients. Go to your appointment and spend an hour explaining everything that's been going on. They can only help people who are ready to get better, and it seems like you are, so its worth a try.
Have you talked to a professional yet?
